rows.subtopic: Handling a legal or tax notice
rows.subtype: Approach: reading the notice carefully and noting the deadline [Thinking]
rows.description: On receiving a tax department email, the person reads who sent it, what is asked and the last date to respond, and does not react until the facts are clear.

rows.subtopic: Handling a legal or tax notice
rows.subtype: Approach: verifying authenticity through official channels [Action]
rows.description: Aware of frauds using fake notices, the person logs in to the official portal directly and checks whether the same notice appears there, rather than clicking email links.

rows.subtopic: Handling a legal or tax notice
rows.subtype: Approach: ignoring the notice from fear [Pitfall]
rows.description: The person puts the letter in a drawer, hoping it is a mistake. The deadline passes, penalties are added, and a simple mismatch becomes a bigger problem.

rows.subtopic: Handling a legal or tax notice
rows.subtype: Approach: revising record-keeping after the episode [Revision]
rows.description: After resolving the matter, the person starts tracking side income and receipts monthly, so that the next filing has complete records and fewer mismatches.

rows.subtype: Approach: taking turns by the clock [Action]
rows.description: Two brothers share one tablet and use a kitchen timer so each gets thirty minutes. The fixed time stops the argument about who has been playing for longer.

rows.subtype: Approach: agreeing to a plan with days for each [Thinking]
rows.description: Siblings agree that Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays are for one, and the rest for the other. They think about fairness and note that some days will suit one child's homework better.

rows.subtype: Approach: grabbing it first and refusing to hand over [Pitfall]
rows.description: An older sister takes the remote and hides it because she got there first. Her brother complains, the parents are upset, and the sharing turns into a fight over power.

rows.subtype: Approach: changing the plan when exams come [Revision]
rows.description: When the older sibling has exams, the children notice the schedule is unfair. They talk and agree that the younger gets more time for two weeks and it will balance later.

rows.subtype: Approach: working backward from the date [Thinking]
rows.description: For a Diwali cultural evening, the student fixes the date, then counts back to book the hall, invite guests, rehearse performances and finalise food, so each step has a deadline.

rows.subtype: Approach: budget and resource planning [Action]
rows.description: The organiser lists all expected costs, sets a limit of what each classmate can contribute, prices alternatives such as home-made snacks, and tracks spending in a shared sheet.

rows.subtype: Approach: last-minute leaving everything to the day [Pitfall]
rows.description: Assuming things will work out, the organisers wait until the final day to arrange sound and seating. Equipment problems and missing chairs cause chaos and disappoint the guests.

rows.subtype: Approach: adapting when things go wrong on the day [Revision]
rows.description: When the chief guest is late, the organiser moves the performance forward and adjusts the order, keeping the audience engaged. Later the team notes a buffer would have helped.

rows.subtype: Approach: identifying the underlying concern behind the demand [Thinking]
rows.description: A wife notices her mother-in-law's insistence on cooking for the family comes from a wish to feel needed. She considers ways to include her rather than only resisting.

rows.subtype: Approach: agreeing with the spouse before speaking to parents [Action]
rows.description: The couple first decides their shared position on visits and holidays. Only then does the husband talk to his parents, so the family sees a united couple, not a spouse against them.

rows.subtype: Approach: avoiding the issue and building resentment [Pitfall]
rows.description: The wife says nothing about frequent unannounced visits. Resentment builds, and one day a minor comment leads to an outburst that hurts everyone far beyond the original matter.

rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing what worked after the festival season [Revision]
rows.description: After a tense Diwali, they note which arrangements helped and which did not. They change next year's plan by hosting one meal and travelling for the other, staying kinder to all.

rows.subtype: Approach: repeating the list aloud again and again [Action]
rows.description: A girl told to bring seven items for a craft class chants them over and over on the way home. It works for a short time, but she forgets two after being interrupted by her brother.

rows.subtype: Approach: asking a parent to remind him at night [Action]
rows.description: Knowing he tends to forget, a boy asks his father to ask him in the evening what is needed. This uses another person as a memory helper for a one-time, important list.

rows.subtype: Approach: trusting memory and not writing it [Pitfall]
rows.description: A girl feels sure that she will remember four items for the school trip. By evening she recalls only three, and has to call a classmate, who is unavailable.

rows.subtype: Approach: testing himself by covering the list [Revision]
rows.description: After checking, a girl finds she missed two items. She covers the list and tries to say all items again, repeating until she can say them all, and then she sleeps on it.

rows.subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
rows.subtype: Approach: thinking of how the owner must feel [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy finds a wallet on the bus and imagines his own father losing one, so he decides the money matters less than getting it back to the owner.

rows.subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
rows.subtype: Approach: pros and cons of keeping it [Thinking]
rows.description: A child lists that keeping the money buys a cricket bat, but the owner might need it for medicine or rent, and that he would feel guilty every time he used it.

rows.subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
rows.subtype: Approach: keeping it because nobody saw [Pitfall]
rows.description: A boy pockets a hundred rupee note on the street thinking no one will know, then spends the day uneasy and is caught by the guilt more than by anyone's eyes.

rows.subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
rows.subtype: Approach: changing mind after temptation [Revision]
rows.description: At first the girl decides to keep the money, but after talking with her friend who says the owner may be poor, she reverses and gives it to the shopkeeper to look after.
